description: A small group of friends, challenging themselves with new ideas
summary: Every week a heatwave, a flood or a cold snap is called “historic” — but which headlines reflect a real trend, and which are just a bad year? Sen-a is a web app where anyone can learn to answer that with real NASA data. Guided by Sen, a sentinel watching over Earth from space, users can research freely or complete short missions: they explore signals like rainfall or sea temperature and learn to tell a clue from a confirmed case. Each finding becomes a star in their constellation, and users review each other’s work, catching mistakes like confusing correlation with causation. Because you don’t need to be a scientist to take part in science.
details:
Context on the problem

We are constantly flooded with stimuli and information: TV, news, social media... These days, everybody is constantly sharing their opinion and hearing such a vast amount of them from others. Earth, of course, along with climate, is one of those factors everyone has an opinion about. Unprecedented disasters seem to be more common: every summer brings a "record" heatwave and every autumn a "historic" flood. Headlines and opinions pull in opposite directions: denial, alarm, or simply more media coverage. What is actually true? Who should we believe?

We are also losing the patience these questions require. The average time people spend on one screen before switching has dropped from 2.5 minutes in 2004 to about 47 seconds today (Gloria Mark, UC Irvine, via APA). And reading data is hard for many of us: only about 37% of US adults can reliably answer a question about a line chart over time (OECD PIAAC 2012–2014, via 3iap). With AI making convincing content cheaper than ever, the noise will only grow. That is why Sen-a's daily challenges take about a minute: short enough to fit our attention, real enough to train it.

Answering that takes skills most people never learn: telling a long-term trend from one unusual year, knowing when a result could be chance, and not confusing two things that move together with one causing the other. NASA's Earth observation data is open to everyone, but for most of us it is not readable.

Without those skills, we end up believing whoever speaks loudest, or we stop listening altogether. The issue is not a lack of data; it is a lack of tools to read it and the amount of voices claiming to be stating the truth.

Solution

Sen-a teaches anyone to read real NASA data and contribute to science, guided by Sen, the sentinel of a space station. Sen never gives orders: she shares what she has seen and asks for help ("From up here I see something strange in this river basin. Can you give me a hand?"). You act as a detective, searching for trends around the globe.

Your first mission: the tutorial

Everyone who signs up starts with the same guided mission. This is how it works:

  1. Meet Sen. She greets you and gives you Mission 00: study the rain around Valencia, hit by the DANA flood in October 2024.
  2. Open your first investigation. Sen guides you step by step: choose a concern (floods), a zone and a period.
  3. Read your first trend. Sea temperature off Valencia rises +0.48 °C per decade (p = 0.0001): a confirmed case. Sen explains trends and p-values in plain words.
  4. Three quick challenges. Spot which signal really rises, tell a clue from a confirmed case, and see why two things moving together don't prove that one causes the other.
  5. Your own verdict. Pick a second signal and judge it yourself. The wettest day of the year in the Poyo river basin is rising, but right at the limit (p = 0.045). Is it a clue or a confirmed case? There is no single right answer; what counts is your reasoning.
  6. Your first constellation. Your findings and your reasoning are saved as stars, joined into your first constellation.
  7. Mission 01: peer review. To present you the peer reviewing feature, you will unlock Mission 01. Sen asks you to check four reports from the crew. One of them makes an incorrect reasoning in their findings. Can you spot it?
After the tutorial
  • Clues and confirmed cases. Every finding is labelled honestly. An honest clue is worth as much as a confirmed case, and ruling out a hypothesis also earns points.
  • Constellations. Like a detective's board joined with red string, each finding is a star, and you connect them into your own constellation. No two are alike. You will create a constellation for each investigation.
  • Peer review. Users check each other's constellations and spot common mistakes, such as confusing correlation with causation. Checking someone else's work is rewarded, not just agreeing with it.
  • Ways to play. Daily challenges of about a minute ("Where is this chart?", a climate GeoGuessr; "Hoax or data?"), weekly missions, and a free research mode for any zone and variable.
Fair-play rules
  • Numbers are generated, never typed: users add their interpretation but cannot change a figure.
  • Every investigation can be reproduced by anyone.
  • Every historical or comparison fact carries its source and date.
  • Sen-a does not predict disasters. It explains trends and risks, and links to official weather services for warnings.

Creativity

Sen-a turns statistics into a game without watering them down. The p-value becomes "could this be chance?". Statistical significance becomes the difference between a clue and a confirmed case. Correlation versus causation becomes a peer-review challenge where you catch someone else's mistake.

The classic detective board becomes a sky: clues are stars and your reasoning draws the constellation. And Sen gives a warm face to a topic that usually arrives wrapped in anxiety. She never scolds, she is happy to see you, and she nudges with humour ("You've repeated a lot of searches in a few minutes. You're not forcing a result, are you?").

Existing tools either open the data or make learning fun, rarely both:

  • NASA Giovanni and Worldview make Earth data open to everyone, but assume you already know how to read it.
  • Learning apps like Duolingo make daily practice fun, but don't work with real data.
  • Climate dashboards show trends already computed for you, without explaining how certain they are.

Sen-a joins all three: real NASA data, a game that teaches you to read it, and a community that checks each other's conclusions.

Impact

Sen-a is for high school and university students, journalists and science communicators, and anyone curious about what is happening around them. No scientific background is needed.

Data literacy, through the 4 Cs

Users learn to read trends, uncertainty and causality in real data, and develop the 4 Cs along the way:

  • Critical thinking. Telling a clue from a confirmed case, asking "could this be chance?", and never confusing correlation with causation.
  • Communication. Writing down your reasoning with every verdict, and sharing constellations that others can follow.
  • Collaboration. Reviewing each other's work and working towards shared crew goals.
  • Creativity. Free research, where you choose the place, the signal and the question, and a constellation that connects the clues your own way.
Beyond the app
  • Community science. With many people studying the same phenomena at the same time, and checking each other, the community learns more than anyone could alone.
  • Against misinformation. Instead of trusting someone else's opinion, users check viral claims against the data themselves and form their own.
  • SDG 4: Quality Education and SDG 13: Climate Action, especially target 13.3 on climate change education and awareness.

You don't need to be a great scientist or part of a research team to contribute to science. It's not someone else's job: this is us, taking care of us.

Relevance to the challenge

The challenge asks for a tool that helps users become data detectives: find variables of interest, see how they change, and decide whether the change is significant. Sen-a is built around exactly that idea.

  • Identifying variables of interest → Users start from a concern (floods, heat, drought…) and Sen-a suggests related NASA variables, each with a simple definition.
  • Acquiring data for a particular region → Users pick a zone on the map; Sen-a explains why each signal is measured where it is (e.g. the sea that feeds autumn storms).
  • Generating and visualizing a time series → Every investigation shows the series over 2001–2024, with the seasonal cycle removed.
  • Rate of change and significance → Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, with 95% confidence intervals and the p-value explained as "could this be chance?"
  • Demonstration examples → A guided first mission that every user shares, plus short daily challenges.
  • A short series of questions about what and where → The investigation starts with three questions: what worries you, where, and over which period.
  • Trends that aren't significant yet → A non-significant trend is a "clue", not a failure: it may become a confirmed case with more years of data.

The MVP covers the full guided onboarding and runs in any phone browser from a QR code, with nothing to install.

Technical description

Sen-a is a web app designed mobile-first, so it works best on a phone but also runs in any browser. We built it with Next.js and React, used Three.js for the spinning Earth and Framer Motion to give Sen and the screens some life, and deployed it on Vercel.

Everything you see is real NASA data. We downloaded it through Giovanni for 2001–2024, around Valencia and the Poyo river basin, where the 2024 flood hit hardest: rainfall from GPM IMERG and sea temperature from MERRA-2. We worked out the trends ourselves with simple, well-established statistics (Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope, plus Spearman correlation to compare signals). In the app we turned all of that into one easy rule: if p is below 0.05, it’s a confirmed case; otherwise, it’s still a clue.

Try it at sen-a.vercel.app. The tutorial comes first and unlocks the rest.

Scientific validity and limitations

Sen-a uses the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope because they make no assumption about how the data is distributed and are robust to outliers. They are standard methods for climate and hydrology time series. Every trend comes with its 95% confidence interval, and seasonal cycles are removed first.

We are open about what the data can and cannot say, and so is Sen:

  • Short records. 24 years (2001–2024) can confirm strong trends but may miss weaker ones. A clue today may become a confirmed case with more years of data.
  • Spatial resolution. Satellite data averages over grid cells (about 10 km for GPM IMERG), not a single street or rain gauge.
  • Many tests, some false alarms. At p < 0.05, about 1 test in 20 looks significant by pure chance. Sen-a warns users who run many searches in a row.
  • One extreme event can weigh a lot. In a series of yearly maximums, a single event like the 2024 DANA can tip the result, so users are prompted to check it.
  • Correlation is not causation. Two signals moving together may share a common cause, as the tutorial shows with Valencia's sea and Bilbao's air.

About the use of SI

SI has been used throughout this project to assist with different tasks, but we would want to remark that no task has been left entirely for the SI to complete. In this team, SI is treated as an assistant, which can help us review specific areas of work. It was used for:

  • Reviewing long texts and correcting grammar or coherence mistakes.
  • Debugging code and looking for reference when faced with complex frontend components.
  • Assisting with video transitions and layering of the different scenes and elements of the storyboard.
  • Refactoring UI components to match specific features by our designer.
  • Having an artist and matching the views of our team, none of the art was made by SI (including images, logos or voice).
